turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll check your blood pressure and weight before Dr Shah sees you. Sleeve up, please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, okay. Um, is he running very late? I've been a bit woozy out there and I keep thinking something's properly wrong.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Only a few minutes. Blood pressure is 118 over 74, pulse 88, weight 67.4 kilos, oxygen 98 percent.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Um, while you're in there, I don't think the iron on the screen is right.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Ferrous sulphate, 200 milligrams, twice a day. Is that what you take?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The bottle at home says 325 milligrams, I'm almost sure. And I don't take two a day. I take one sometimes, if I remember, maybe a couple of times a week.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): I'll flag that. Any allergies? The record says none.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no allergies. Well, actually, I don't think so, nothing I know of. Sorry, can I ask, will he want to examine me down below? I get really anxious about examinations.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): He'll say if he needs to. I'll call him.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mrs Adeyemi? Dr Shah. What's the main problem today?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm exhausted. Properly exhausted. And I get breathless just walking in from the car park. And my periods are a nightmare.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the periods been heavy?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): About a year. Maybe a bit more. I lose track, sorry.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pads per day?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't count properly. Loads. On a bad day six or seven, sometimes I just keep changing them. It's a guess, really.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Clots?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, big ones, though I can't really say how big — not little dots. Is that useless, sorry?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hair coming out?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, in the shower and on the pillow. My sister takes biotin for her hair and she keeps pushing it on me, but I haven't taken any. They're her tablets.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain at all.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Cough? Fever?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough, and no fever.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Palpitations?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Now and again, when I'm rushing about. Not constantly. Does that mean my heart's packing up?
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chance you're pregnant?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not. My husband had the snip years ago.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thyroid trouble yourself?

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. My mum's got an underactive thyroid and she's always on at me. And my husband takes metformin for his diabetes — he says I've got it too, which is daft, I barely eat sweets. Sorry, that's not helpful.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the tiredness start?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you. Months, maybe. It crept up. I can't put a date on it.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Breathlessness — how long?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): More recent, the last three weeks or so, worse on the stairs. I can still speak in full sentences, I'm doing it now, aren't I? The nursery stairs are the worst, I stop halfway and pretend I'm hunting for a hair clip.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Are you taking the iron every day?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, like I said, only sometimes — I forget, and some weeks I hardly touch it. Is that making me worse, have I damaged something?
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Heavy periods for a year, likely low iron. I'll put the ferrous sulphate up to 200 milligrams twice a day and see you in six weeks. No scan.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks? I can't do six weeks. Yesterday in Tesco the room went funny and I had to sit on the floor, and the clots have been worse this month. Is it cancer, do I need a transfusion?
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you black out?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Not fully. Everything went grey and I sat down, then it passed. It really frightened me. Should I be in hospital?
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not hospital today. That changes things. Forget the six weeks, and I won't increase the iron until we know what the bloods show — the dose doesn't even match.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): So what happens now? Am I anaemic? Is it my heart? Could it be the thyroid like my mum?

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I suspect anaemia from the heavy bleeding, though I can't confirm it without bloods, and I wouldn't rule out a thyroid problem. We'll do a full blood count, ferritin and thyroid function today, and I'll see you in two weeks. We might do a pelvic scan if the bleeding hasn't settled by then.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the scan the internal one, will it hurt? If the bloods are normal do I still come, and can I work? I'm in a nursery, on my feet all day.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): If we scan, it'll be an external one first. Come back in two weeks either way. Work if you feel up to it, and sit down if you feel faint.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I keep taking my iron, the sometimes one? And would my sister's biotin help the hair at all?
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Keep taking your own iron as you have been until the results. Don't take her biotin. It isn't your medicine and it won't sort this.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I flood a pad really quickly, or I actually pass out next time?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you're soaking through a pad every hour, or you collapse, or you get chest pain, go to A&E. Otherwise it's two weeks.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Sorry, last one. Will someone do the bloods now? I hate needles, I might go woozy again.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): I can do them straight after. Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid, as Dr Shah said. Quick scratch.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Two weeks. If anything else occurs to you, catch the nurse on the way out.

spec.situation: Tired, breathless woman with heavy periods for a year; counts pads and clots in vague terms; takes iron 'sometimes'; hair loss; relative mentions thyroid in the family. Blood tests, maybe pelvic scan.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Transcript mentions husband's diabetes, not family history.
Wooziness present, but severity 'mild' is not stated.
bad.text: wooziness (category=neurological, status=present, severity=mild, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Ferrous sulphate dose is recorded incompletely/wrongly: the patient said the bottle at home says 325 mg, and she takes 1 tablet only sometimes, maybe a couple of times a week; the on-screen record of 200 mg twice daily was disputed.

The doctor explicitly changed the initial plan: after hearing about the near-faint episode, he said to forget the 6-week follow-up and that he would not increase the iron until the blood results are known.
Near-faint episode details are incomplete: yesterday in Tesco the room 'went funny', everything went grey, she had to sit on the floor, it passed, and it frightened her; she did not fully black out.
Breathlessness detail missing: she can still speak in full sentences despite the breathlessness.
Negative finding missing: no known personal history of thyroid trouble ('Not that I know of').
